analysis.one_liner: Lets states tax self-insured health plans to fund universal coverage and care for the uninsurable.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in October 1992, sent to a House committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law (ERISA) currently stops states from making self-insured employer health plans pay state health care taxes or join state risk pools. This bill would waive that rule, letting states tax or surcharge all health plans equally to pay for universal health plans, insurance pools for people too sick to buy coverage, and hospital payment systems that charge for care given to the poor. It died in committee with no votes and no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: State residents who are uninsured or medically uninsurable would gain, because states could finance risk pools and broader coverage programs with taxes on all health plans, including self-insured employer plans that currently escape such state levies. States would gain new freedom to design and fund their own health systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured residents of states that act

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA so a state's universal health plan, risk pool for the medically uninsurable, or prospective payment system can apply to self-insured employer plans, which are currently shielded from state health care financing rules [S3].

States could impose taxes or premium surcharges on health plans doing business in the state, as long as the tax does not discriminate among plans by type or size, and use the proceeds to finance a state risk pool for the medically uninsurable or to significantly expand residents' access to cost-effective care [S3].

States could also impose nondiscriminatory broad-based health care taxes on providers and set hospital rates prospectively, including charges for uncompensated care such as care for the indigent and bad debts [S3].

A state plan would qualify only if the Secretary of Health and Human Services finds it has sufficient resources and capacity to accomplish its goals, with reporting on the results of the first approved plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with self-insured health plans, which cover a large share of insured workers, would pay the new state taxes or surcharges and could pass some of that cost to workers through premiums. Health care providers would pay broad-based state health care taxes.

drawbacks.text: Taxes or surcharges on employer health plans, including self-insured plans, would raise the cost of job-based coverage, and employers could shift part of that cost to workers through premiums [S3].

The bill only opens a door: each state program must be approved by the Secretary of Health and Human Services and meet federal uniformity standards, so nothing guarantees any state actually establishes universal coverage [S3].
Health care providers would bear a new broad-based state tax burden, which could contribute to higher prices for care [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: federal law lets self-insured employer plans avoid state health care financing taxes while free-riding on state programs that care for the uninsured. Waiving that shield would have given states a workable way to fund coverage for people who cannot get insurance. The main cost is higher financing burdens on employer plans and providers, which could reach workers and patients through premiums and prices, and the bill guaranteed nothing on its own since states still had to design and win approval for programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, and then sent to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli introduced the bill on October 3, 1992, near the end of the 102nd Congress [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S5].
On October 9, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and no further action was taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Self-insured employers and health plans remain exempt from state health care financing taxes, so the cost of caring for the uninsured continues to fall elsewhere; no state gained the option this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Self-insured employers keep their tax exemption

for.name: Rep. Romano L. Mazzoli
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to waive ERISA preemption for state health financing programs; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations and never acted on it, so it received no markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes or recorded opposition, the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.note: These plans are currently exempt from state health care taxes and risk pool participation under ERISA. The bill would have made them pay the same state levies as other plans, ending a free ride on programs that care for the uninsured.

Insured plans would face the same state taxes they may already face, but the bill required state levies to be uniform, so insurers would no longer be the only plans paying for state risk pools and universal coverage programs.

The bill would let states set hospital rates prospectively with charges for uncompensated care, including indigent care and bad debts, and states could finance expanded access programs that increase paying demand, though providers would also face broad-based state health taxes.
